lead: Pipelining cuts a long block of logic into stages with registers between them, so a new input can start every short clock period instead of every long one: throughput rises, at the cost of some latency and some registers. The same syllabus topic groups the nonbistable sequential circuits, circuits with feedback that do not have two stable states: the Schmitt trigger with its two thresholds, the monostable one-shot that makes a pulse of fixed width, and the astable ring oscillator that never stops switching.
prereq: You need: register timing (setup time, clock-to-Q) from Chapter 4.6, and the multiplier of Chapter 4.4 for the example datapath.

blocks.text: Take a multiply-accumulate step, y = a × b + c, applied to a stream of samples. Without pipelining, an input register launches a, b and c, the multiplier and then the adder settle, and an output register captures y. The clock period must cover the whole path: T = t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>mult</sub> + t<sub>add</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>.
Put a register after the multiplier. Now the multiplier works on sample n + 1 while the adder finishes sample n, and each stage only needs its own logic in one period:
Here t<sub>stage,max</sub> is the logic delay of the slowest stage; t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>su</sub> is the register overhead that every stage pays once.

Two numbers describe a pipeline. Throughput is results per second, 1 ÷ T<sub>pipe</sub> once the pipeline is full. Latency is the time from an input to its result: k × T<sub>pipe</sub> for k stages. Latency grows, because every stage pays the overhead and waits for the slowest stage. N inputs take (k + N − 1) periods: k to fill the pipeline, then one result per period. So k stages are at most k times faster, and only when the stages are balanced and the overhead is small.

A register cannot be dropped into a feedback loop, such as an accumulator adding its own output, because the loop would then use an older value. Latch-based pipelines use two-phase latches instead of registers, so a slow stage can borrow time from the next. NORA CMOS is a dynamic logic style built for this: alternating n-type and p-type dynamic blocks with C<sup>2</sup>MOS latches between them.

A Schmitt trigger is an inverter or buffer with two switching thresholds. A rising input switches it at V<sub>M+</sub>; a falling input switches it back only below V<sub>M−</sub>, with V<sub>M+</sub> > V<sub>M−</sub>. The gap V<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>M+</sub> − V<sub>M−</sub> is the hysteresis, and the transfer characteristic is a loop rather than one curve. Noise smaller than V<sub>H</sub> cannot make the output chatter, and a slow, noisy ramp gives one clean, fast edge (worked example 2). Input pins, reset lines and switch debouncers use one.

The CMOS Schmitt trigger is an inverter with positive feedback. In the common six-transistor form the pull-down is two nMOS in series, and a feedback nMOS, gated by the output, connects their middle node towards V<sub>DD</sub>. While the output is high, that transistor holds the middle node up, so the input must rise further before the pull-down wins: V<sub>M+</sub> moves up. A matching feedback pMOS on the two series pMOS lowers V<sub>M−</sub> while the output is low. Sizing the feedback transistors sets the hysteresis.

A monostable circuit, or one-shot, has one stable state. A trigger edge flips it into the other state and it returns by itself after a fixed time, so its output is a pulse of set width. The CMOS version needs no capacitor: feed the input to an AND gate directly and through a chain of an odd number N of inverters. After a rising edge the delayed, inverted copy stays 1 for the chain delay, so the AND gives a pulse of width about N × tp, where tp is one inverter's delay. An XOR of the input and a delayed copy pulses on both edges; memories use that as address transition detection (Chapter 4.10).

An astable circuit has no stable state and oscillates by itself. The ring oscillator is an odd number N of inverters in a loop: no set of values is consistent, so a transition runs round the ring for ever. One period needs the edge to go round twice, once rising and once falling:

blocks.where: N is the odd number of inverters and t<sub>p</sub> the propagation delay of one inverter. An even ring has a consistent state, so it is a latch, not an oscillator.

blocks.text: Starving each inverter of current through a control voltage turns the ring into a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) for phase-locked loops. A relaxation oscillator, a capacitor charged until a Schmitt trigger flips and discharges it, is another astable circuit.

examples.question: A multiply-accumulate datapath has t<sub>mult</sub> = 3.0 ns and t<sub>add</sub> = 1.6 ns. Every register has t<sub>cq</sub> = 0.2 ns and t<sub>su</sub> = 0.1 ns. Find the clock period, clock frequency and latency (a) without pipelining, (b) with one register after the multiplier, (c) with the multiplier also split into two 1.5 ns halves. (d) How long does design (c) take for 1000 samples, against design (a)?
steps: (b) Stages are 3.0 ns and 1.6 ns. T = 0.2 + 3.0 + 0.1 = 3.3 ns, so f = 303.0 MHz. Latency = 2 × 3.3 = 6.6 ns. Speed-up = 4.9 ÷ 3.3 = 1.48, far from 2, because the stages are unbalanced.

(c) Stages are 1.5, 1.5 and 1.6 ns. T = 0.2 + 1.6 + 0.1 = 1.9 ns, so f = 526.3 MHz. Latency = 3 × 1.9 = 5.7 ns. Speed-up = 4.9 ÷ 1.9 = 2.58, not 3, because each stage pays 0.3 ns of overhead and the adder stage is 0.1 ns slower than the others.
examples.answer: Unpipelined: 4.9 ns, 204.1 MHz, latency 4.9 ns. Two stages: 3.3 ns, 303.0 MHz, latency 6.6 ns. Three stages: 1.9 ns, 526.3 MHz, latency 5.7 ns; 1000 samples take 1903.8 ns instead of 4900 ns.

examples.question: A slow, noisy input is sampled at ten instants: 0.20, 0.60, 0.95, 0.85, 0.98, 1.20, 1.05, 0.95, 1.40, 1.70 V. It drives (a) a plain inverter with V<sub>M</sub> = 0.9 V and (b) a Schmitt trigger inverter with V<sub>M+</sub> = 1.1 V and V<sub>M−</sub> = 0.7 V. Both outputs start high. How many output edges does each give?
steps: Plain inverter: the output is low whenever the input is above 0.9 V. Samples 1 to 2 are below (high), 3 is above (low), 4 is below (high), 5 to 10 are above (low).
So the plain inverter switches at sample 3, back at sample 4 and again at sample 5: three edges where there should be one.
Schmitt trigger: with the output high it switches low only when the input rises above V<sub>M+</sub> = 1.1 V. That first happens at sample 6 (1.20 V).
With the output low it switches back only below V<sub>M−</sub> = 0.7 V. After sample 6 the lowest sample is 0.95 V, so it stays low.
Hysteresis V<sub>H</sub> = 0.4 V is larger than the noise.
examples.answer: The plain inverter gives three edges (two of them false); the Schmitt trigger gives one clean edge, at sample 6.

traps: Saying pipelining reduces latency. It raises throughput; latency grows, since every stage pays the register overhead and waits for the slowest stage.
Expecting k times the speed from k stages. Register overhead and unbalanced stages always take some of it (2.58 instead of 3 in worked example 1).
Mixing up the thresholds: V<sub>M+</sub> is the higher one, crossed by a rising input; the hysteresis is V<sub>M+</sub> − V<sub>M−</sub>.
Ring oscillator frequency is 1 ÷ (2N·t<sub>p</sub>), not 1 ÷ (N·t<sub>p</sub>): the edge must go round twice per period. N must be odd.

quiz.q: Define throughput and latency for a pipeline.
quiz.a: Throughput is the number of results per second, 1 ÷ T<sub>pipe</sub> once the pipeline is full. Latency is the time from an input entering to its result leaving, k × T<sub>pipe</sub> for k stages.

quiz.q: What is hysteresis in a Schmitt trigger?
quiz.a: The difference between its two switching thresholds, V<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>M+</sub> − V<sub>M−</sub>. The rising input switches it at V<sub>M+</sub>, the falling input at the lower V<sub>M−</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does a three-stage pipeline not run three times faster than the unpipelined datapath?
quiz.a: Each stage adds register overhead t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>, and the clock must suit the slowest stage. Unless the stages are perfectly balanced and the overhead is negligible, T<sub>pipe</sub> is more than one third of the old period.

quiz.q: A ring oscillator has 5 inverters, each with t<sub>p</sub> = 20 ps. Find its frequency.
A one-shot uses an AND gate and a chain of 7 inverters of 30 ps each. Estimate the output pulse width after a rising input edge.
quiz.a: The delayed, inverted input stays 1 for the chain delay: 7 × 30 ps = 210 ps, so the pulse is about 210 ps wide (plus the AND gate delay at each edge).

quiz.q: A signal sits at 0.9 V with ±0.15 V of noise. Compare a plain inverter with V<sub>M</sub> = 0.9 V and a Schmitt trigger with V<sub>M+</sub> = 1.1 V and V<sub>M−</sub> = 0.7 V.
quiz.a: The input wanders between 0.75 V and 1.05 V. The plain inverter switches every time it crosses 0.9 V, so its output chatters. The Schmitt trigger never reaches 1.1 V or 0.7 V, so its output does not change: noise smaller than the 0.4 V hysteresis is ignored.

beyond: Not for the exam. Processors pipeline instructions in many stages with hazard detection and forwarding, and on-chip clock generators are phase-locked loops built around current-starved ring oscillators. Search next for "retiming" and "ring-oscillator VCO".
